Any of the rodents of the family Sciuridae.
d.x: tree squirrels

d.g: Any of those distinguished typically by a large bushy tail; any of the tree squirrels of subfamily Sciurinae or phenotypically similar sciurids.
Someone who displays squirrel-like qualities such as stealing or hoarding objects.
One of the small rollers of a carding machine which work with the large cylinder.

squirrel.e: From Middle English squirel, squyrelle, from Anglo-Norman esquirel and Old French escurel (whence French écureuil), from Vulgar Latin *scūriolus, diminutive of *scūrius, variant of Latin sciūrus, from Ancient Greek σκίουρος (skíouros, “shadow-tail”, from σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”)). …

d.g: Any member of the subfamily Holocentrinae of the family Holocentridae of ray-finned fish.
A sand perch (Diplectrum)
An instrument from which a liquid is forcefully ejected in a small, quick stream.
A small, quick stream; a jet.
d.x: Chances are you′ll get a squirt of citrus juice in your eye.

d.g: The whole system of flow in the vicinity of a source.
A burst of noise.
d.x: As the connection was broken, the receiver let out a shrill squirt of static.

squirt.e: From Middle English squirten, squyrten, of uncertain origin; probably onomatopoeic. Akin to swirl. Compare Low German swirtjen (“to squirt”) and Swedish water onomatopoeias skvala, skvalp, skvimpa, and skvätta; Icelandic skvetta; and Norwegian skvette.

d.g: One who, or that which, squirts.
d.x: When a surface is not easily accessible or is not flat, a water squirter is sometimes used.

d.g: A woman who can ejaculate.
A person, presumed to be hostile, who absconds upon the approach of (Western) soldiers.
d.x: Who made the decision to send an IRF after a group of squirters?

squirter.e: English squirt English -er English squirter From squirt + -er.

d.g: The sound or action of something, especially something moist, being squeezed or crushed.
d.x: Alex reached the bottom and Grant heard a squish as she landed in the mud on the bottom of the river.

d.g: A political moderate.
d.x: Some conservatives think that in the long run, the party will be better off without squishes like Specter […]

d.g: To squeeze, compress, or crush (especially something moist).
d.x: The sandwich tasted fine, even though it had got squished in his lunchbox.

d.g: To be compressed or squeezed.
d.x: I kicked off my shoes and wiggled my toes on the soft moss. It felt amazing as it squished between my toes, […]

squish.e: Apparently an alteration of squash, influenced by obsolete squiss (“to squeeze”). Cognate with Scots squische, squies (“to crush, squeeze”). Compare also French esquicher from Old Occitan esquichar (“to squeeze, squish”). See also squeeze, squelch.

d.g: To waste, lavish, splurge; to spend lavishly or profusely; to dissipate.

squander.e: Earliest uses (late 16th c.) "to spend recklessly or prodigiously", also "to scatter over a wide area". Of unknown origin. Perhaps a blend of scatter + wander. …
